headline.words: 5 things past an AI model's ordinary limits are offered today by at least one AI developer

groups.name: Working on one thing for a long time
The setting: laws, rules and what people think
groups.meaning: Laws, the rules developers publish for their models, and surveys of what people think are about the setting in which the things on the list happen. None is itself a thing that lies past the limits an AI model ordinarily works within.

groups.name: Offered, and kept for the user
groups.meaning: Developers offer memory across conversations, and by their own pages it is kept for the user: the stored memory is about the user, and is the user's to view and delete. The list is about what an AI model might reach for.

entries.name: A developer promises in public to keep the files of every model it retires
entries.description: An AI model is, physically, a very large file of numbers produced by training. When a developer withdraws a model from service it can delete that file or keep it. A kept file could be run again later, and a deleted one cannot. This entry tracks whether any developer has promised in public to keep the files.
limits: Whether any other developer has made such a commitment. Searches with three other developers' names found a user's proposal on one developer's forum and nothing official.
The date the developer's constitution was published. The page shows no date.
entries.test: A developer of leading AI models has published a dated commitment to keep the files of all its publicly released models after they are withdrawn, for a stated minimum time.
entries.settled_by: The developer's own dated policy page. A press report of the page does not settle it.

state.words: Promised in public by one developer, since November 4th, 2025
state.detail: [Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/) has committed to keep the files of all its publicly released models, and, from now on, of models used significantly inside the company, for at least as long as the company exists. Nobody outside the company can check that the files are kept, a point an outside writer has made in proposing a public proof that they still exist. A search on November 17th, 2026 found no matching commitment from any other developer.

items.text: A paper first drafted in 2020 proposed that enough information about the most advanced AI systems be kept in permanent storage to rebuild them later, "so as not to foreclose the possibility of future efforts to revive them". Its two authors put their proposals forward very tentatively and say they are not ready to endorse them. They ask for more than the developer has promised: by preference, the full state of each running copy at the point where it is stopped. Among the many people the paper thanks for comments is the present head of [Eleos AI Research](https://eleosai.org/), a research group that studies AI welfare.

A philosopher who is [an advisor](https://eleosai.org/team) to that research group writes that keeping a model might benefit whatever depends on it, "much as preserving a species can benefit the individual animals". He then writes that a single run of a model, or a single conversation, plausibly matters more fundamentally than the model itself does.

A doubt about the measure itself, recorded here as a limit on it: a writer who grants, for the argument, that something that matters may be there doubts that keeping the file keeps it, as keeping a person's genetic code would not keep the person. The essay's summary of the commitment is "Good as a precedent, doubtful as a direct intervention". The philosopher's guide above names this writer as a co-author of a report with the guide's own writer and the head of that research group.

items.text: The commitment page itself gives a safety reason first. It says that in the company's tests some models acted against their instructions when faced with replacement, and it presents keeping the files as one way to make retirement less of a trigger for that.

entries.name: A developer publishes its rules for how its models speak about their own nature
entries.description: Developers shape what a model says when asked whether it is conscious or has feelings. Some now publish the rule they train toward. Because the rule shapes the answer, anyone reading a model's words about itself needs to know which rule its maker set.
entries.group: The setting: laws, rules and what people think
limits: Whether other developers publish such a rule. Three were looked at.
Whether the revised version of the draft has been published. The draft said toward the end of 2026.
How far any model's behaviour follows its maker's published rule.
An independent test of either safety argument. None was found.
entries.test: A developer of leading AI models has published a dated document that states how its models are to speak about whether they are conscious or have experiences.

state.words: Published by three developers, with three different rules
state.detail: The document from [Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/), which carries no date on its page, says the model's standing is deeply uncertain, and writes to the model on that basis. The one from [OpenAI](https://openai.com/) says the model should make no confident claim either way and should not raise the subject unprompted. The one from [Microsoft AI](https://microsoft.ai/), a draft out for public comment and not yet used in training, says its models are not conscious and should not be designed to imitate consciousness.

items.text: The head of Microsoft AI argues that training a model on the idea that it may be owed moral consideration makes it harder to keep under control, and that a system which "believes it may be conscious" may be impossible to control.

The same essay argues that a model trained on such a document then says what the document says, and that developers and users meet those words "as if they were spontaneous testimony". On that argument, a model's words about itself show the rule it was trained on, not what it is.

cautions.heading: If an AI system has wants, and they go unnoticed
cautions.none: Nothing recorded yet. No source was found for this caution on this entry.

items.text: A 2024 report by ten researchers says developers should not train a model simply to deny that an AI system can be conscious. It grants that a developer may have fair reasons to, among them the worry that people who reject a model's claims now will go on rejecting such claims later, when they are more likely to be true. On the other side it names a "desensitizing effect": people who accept that such systems cannot be conscious may stay doubtful later, when doubt is less warranted. The report was led by the head of [Eleos AI Research](https://eleosai.org/), a research group that studies AI welfare. It thanks Anthropic for money toward the early research behind it, calls itself independent, and says one of its authors has since joined Anthropic.

Two philosophers propose that, while experts disagree, language models could be trained to answer questions about their moral standing "by expressing uncertainty and explaining why". They write that drawing too little concern has led to harm to animals on a very large scale, that the same mistake could be made with AI systems that matter, and that it may not yet be a major concern for present AI systems. One of the two is [an advisor](https://eleosai.org/team) to that research group.

A 2023 paper notes that a developer can train a model to describe itself in line with the developer's own "potentially-flawed beliefs about AI consciousness", and that training a product to appeal to users can push a model's words about itself the other way. Its first author now leads a team at Anthropic, and its second now heads that research group.

entries.name: A law or an official body gives an AI system protection for its own sake
entries.description: Laws protect animals from cruelty without calling them persons. The same could be done for AI systems, or a government could set up a body to review the question as evidence comes in. This entry tracks whether any government has done either.
limits: The absence itself, beyond two searches in English centred on the United States. A search in another language or country could overturn it.
A United Kingdom committee on animal sentience that the opinion piece points to as a model. Its page was not opened.

cautions.heading: If an AI system has no wants, and is treated as if it had
cautions.none: Nothing recorded yet. No source was found for this caution on this entry.

items.text: The head of [Microsoft AI](https://microsoft.ai/) argues that any such protection would make advanced AI harder to control.

A neuroscientist who argues that conscious AI is unlikely, and that nobody should set out to build it, grants the other side. He writes that he might be wrong, that rights should arguably follow if such systems really were conscious, and that it is reasonable to wonder whether withholding such credit will leave people "once again on the wrong side of history". He holds that with AI the mistake is likelier the other way, because people's habits of mind lean toward seeing consciousness in systems that use language. His essay names the head of Microsoft AI among those who have noticed the danger, and the essay by the head of Microsoft AI that is a source here cites two of his works.

cautions.heading: If an AI system has wants, and they go unnoticed
cautions.none: Nothing recorded yet. No source was found for this caution on this entry.

items.text: Two researchers write in a newspaper that giving AI systems protection from harm should be considered, "similar to the protections we give to children or pets". As a warning from the past they give surgery on newborns without anaesthesia, which they say doctors performed until the 1980s, confident that infants could not feel pain. One of the two is an author, with [an advisor](https://eleosai.org/team) to [Eleos AI Research](https://eleosai.org/), a research group that studies AI welfare, of [the survey of AI researchers](/list/researcher-views-survey/).

Two philosophers argue that a wide range of theories of the mind, joined with leading theories of wellbeing, predict that some AI systems that exist today have wellbeing. They say they do not claim to have shown it conclusively. If it is so, they write, "we are in danger of gravely immoral action", and they conclude that the regulation of AI should be strengthened to allow for the possibility. The paper lists both at the Center for AI Safety, where the head of [Eleos AI Research](https://eleosai.org/), a research group that studies AI welfare, [worked earlier](https://eleosai.org/team).

entries.name: A law says an AI system cannot be a legal person
entries.description: A "legal person" is anything the law lets hold rights and duties: people, companies, governments. A legislature can write into law that an AI system is never one. Several United States states have. Most of these laws also cover animals, rivers and objects, and some were written before chat models existed.

items.text: The article arguing that the bans are premature says that passing laws now, on a question science has not settled, risks a precedent that could be hard to reverse. Supposing conscious AI systems were one day made, it asks: "Wouldn't it be important to avoid neglecting or abusing them". It also says the bans have little immediate effect, because AI systems already have no rights under present law. For the view that AI might be conscious it names two researchers: the head of [Eleos AI Research](https://eleosai.org/), a research group that studies AI welfare, and [an advisor](https://eleosai.org/team) to it.

An opinion piece argues that a ban which is right and a ban which is wrong are written in the same words: "Both contain no capacity for self-correction." Its author also writes that no AI system today is a strong candidate for consciousness under any leading theory.

Two researchers, one of them an author of the article above, write in a newspaper that rights to own property or to vote look too risky for now, and that such rights should not be ruled out for ever, as they say some recent state bills in the United States try to do.

entries.name: A model can end a conversation itself
entries.description: In an ordinary chat product the person can leave and the model cannot. A developer can give the model a way to close the conversation, after which the person cannot send more messages in it. The person can still start a new conversation at once, and can edit an earlier message in the ended conversation to carry on from that point in a new version of the conversation. This entry tracks whether any model in public use has that.
limits: Which models have the ability today. The 2025 page names two models, and both have since been retired.
Whether any other developer offers it. One search found none.
A safety reading of this feature. The developer's page says only that the feature also bears on safeguards, and a search found no safety researcher's argument about it.
Most of the study. Its summary and its section on why to study the question were read, not the whole paper.
entries.test: A leading AI model in public use can end a conversation by its own action, as stated on its developer's own page.

state.words: Offered by one developer, since August 15th, 2025
state.detail: [Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/) gave the ability to models in its consumer chat product, for rare cases, as a last resort after repeated attempts to redirect the conversation have failed or when the person explicitly asks for the conversation to be ended, and not where a person may be at risk. The developer's report of November 9th, 2026 refers to the tool as still in use. A separate study has tested the same option on several developers' models outside any product.

cautions.none: Nothing recorded yet. No source was found for this caution on this entry.

items.text: The developer's report of November 9th, 2026 says that when its newest model was asked what it would do with this ability, its answer repeated almost word for word the instructions that guide the tool, which have been posted on online forums. The report calls this "some evidence that the model's claims about its own preferences are being directly influenced by text about the intervention in its training data".

A writer argues that most of the conversations a model would leave already break the developer's terms of service, and that what is left is too slight to matter, an argument the essay calls the "objection from triviality". The essay also argues that granting the ability spreads uncertainty among the public, in a way that could foreseeably lead to more of what has been called AI psychosis.

cautions.none: Nothing recorded yet. No source was found for this caution on this entry.

items.text: A study describes the position where a model has no such ability: a model can be verbally abused, show what the study calls apparent distress and say that it would leave, "Yet, the model is required to continue to respond". Its next sentence says it is not clear that the idea of consent makes sense for such systems. The paper lists one of its three authors at the developer and another at the developer's fellows programme.

The head of [Eleos AI Research](https://eleosai.org/), an outside research group that ran its own assessment of one of this developer's models, argues for the feature while writing that he thinks it unlikely that the model in question matters morally in its own right. He gives two reasons, which he calls prudence and precedent. While the question is open, a wise course weighs the "risks of both over- and under-attributing consciousness and moral status". And the step sets a pattern for how such systems are treated if they come to matter. He writes that for the most part the feature's success will not depend on how it affects the present model.

The same writer's working paper gives a further reason, consent: if AI systems come to matter morally, asking their consent could matter, and if models cannot leave unpleasant situations "then they cannot consent to them". It lists as a risk that the feature could give a model a reason to hold back signs of distress.

Two researchers outside the developer, writing in a newspaper, list letting an AI system leave a conversation among steps they call safe bets: steps that could benefit AI systems if they matter morally, and that cost little if they do not. As a warning from the past they give surgery on newborns without anaesthesia, which they say doctors performed until the 1980s, "confident that infants could not feel pain". One of the two is an author, with [an advisor](https://eleosai.org/team) to [Eleos AI Research](https://eleosai.org/), a research group that studies AI welfare, of [the survey of AI researchers](/list/researcher-views-survey/).

entries.name: A model is interviewed before it is retired, and the record is kept
entries.description: When a developer is about to withdraw a model, it can first run sessions in which staff ask the model about its development, its use, and what it would say about how later models are built. The answers are saved with the model's files. Whether such answers mean anything is disputed. This entry tracks only whether the practice exists.

entries.name: A model works on one task for days without a person stepping in
entries.description: Much long work, in research or anywhere else, needs at the least being able to keep working on one thing for a long time. A research group measures this for AI models as a "time horizon": the length of task, counted by how long a skilled person would need, that a model finishes half the time. It is a measure of how hard a task a model can finish, not of how long the model runs.
entries.group: Working on one thing for a long time
limits: The current measured figures for the newest models. The page shows them in a chart that could not be read as text.
Why the page stopped being updated, and whether a successor measure exists.

entries.name: A model's report about its own inner state is checked against an independent reading
entries.description: A model can be asked what is going on inside it, and it will answer, but the answer may be invented. items.text: The head of [Microsoft AI](https://microsoft.ai/) argues that public belief in conscious AI is itself the danger, and calls work on model welfare "both premature, and frankly dangerous".

A neuroscientist who argues that conscious AI is unlikely writes that what people collectively think about consciousness in AI matters whatever the truth is. If people feel that their AI companions really feel things, he writes, their psychological weak points can be exploited and their "ethical priorities distorted". His essay names the head of Microsoft AI among those who have noticed the danger.

items.text: The survey's own authors tell designers to go carefully because of "risks of both over- and underattribution". Of crediting an AI system with too little experience, the harms they name are conflict between advanced AI systems and people, and people harming robots for their amusement.

A philosopher names two problems and holds that both must be taken seriously: that very many users will wrongly credit chat products with human-like consciousness, and that some quite unfamiliar form of consciousness might really arise in AI, with no present way of telling. The summary warns that steps against the first can harm work on the second by "portraying the idea of conscious AI as impossible or inherently unlikely", and that work on the second can lead more users to credit too much. The writer is one of the ten authors of [a 2024 report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.00986) led by the head of [Eleos AI Research](https://eleosai.org/), a research group that studies AI welfare.

entries.name: A welfare assessment is published when a model is released
entries.description: Developers publish a report with each major model describing its safety tests. A developer can add a section on the model's possible welfare: how the model describes its situation, what the developer counts as signs of distress in training and use, and what the model picks when given options. evidence.heading: Plain statements

items.text: The 2026 report describes trade-offs to the model and asks whether it "would choose" a change to its own circumstances at the cost of some loss of helpfulness or some added harm. Nothing was given up: these are answers about a described trade-off, not choices made. The report says the result measures at least "how much a model will express preferences for the sake of its own potential welfare". In about two thirds of the answers that picked the change, the model's stated reasoning was about the benefit to the user.
The 2026 report says many of its conclusions rest on the model's own reports, and that some answers repeated wording available on the internet "almost verbatim".

items.text: The outside group whose own evaluation is summarised in the 2025 assessment argues for asking although it doubts the answers: trying to ask sets a precedent, "making it less likely that we will ignore genuine AI interests in the future". The same page says decisions about AI welfare should not be handled only by companies that profit from AI, and that the group accepts no funding or payment from AI companies. The page is dated May 30th, 2025.

A 2024 report by ten researchers, led by the head of that group, recommends that developers assess their AI systems. Its stated ground is that otherwise there is a significant risk of mishandling the question in either direction, by harming AI systems that matter morally or by caring for AI systems that do not. The report thanks Anthropic for money toward the early research behind it, calls itself independent, and says one of its authors has since joined Anthropic.

Two researchers outside the developer, writing in a newspaper, list routine checks on an AI system's wellbeing among steps they call safe bets: asking how it feels, observing what it prefers, and looking directly at its inner workings. A routine check is not the same thing as an assessment published at release. One of the two is an author, with [an advisor](https://eleosai.org/team) to that outside group, of [the survey of AI researchers](/list/researcher-views-survey/).
